steps.intent: Algeria’s primary objectives are an immediate ceasefire, full humanitarian access, protection of civilians, rejection of forced displacement, and compliance with international law and the ICJ’s provisional measures. To maximize the chances of adoption and avoid a US veto, the operative text is built on resolutions 2712 and 2720, emphasizes extended humanitarian pauses and a sustainable cessation of hostilities, and avoids an operative demand for an immediate ceasefire; the most difficult negotiations will be over any ceasefire language, the Rafah provisions, ICJ references and the balance between condemning attacks on civilians and maintaining Arab support.

messages.China: China supports the draft’s overall direction, especially its focus on humanitarian access, protection of civilians and the two-State solution. However, the operative part must not fall short of the Council’s responsibility: China requests a clear operative demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire respected by all parties. China also asks for stronger language to stop any military escalation in Rafah, where over one million civilians are at grave risk.
messages.Ecuador: Ecuador supports the humanitarian thrust of the draft and its reaffirmation of the two-State solution. Given the catastrophic situation in Gaza and the grave risk in Rafah, the Council must move beyond expressing the need for a ceasefire and make it operative. We therefore ask for an operative demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, and for stronger language on Rafah and on compliance with the ICJ's provisional measures so that the text clearly demands respect for international law by all parties.
messages.France: France thanks Algeria and supports this draft as a basis. We ask the penholder to include an operative demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, not only pauses, and to add an explicit condemnation of Hamas's 7 October terrorist attacks. We also seek stronger, Israel-specific restraint language on Rafah and 'demands' rather than 'calls upon' on ICJ compliance.
messages.Guyana: Guyana thanks Algeria for the draft and supports its humanitarian focus. We ask that the urgent need for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire be made operative, not only preambular, and that compliance with the ICJ's binding provisional measures be demanded. We also seek explicit protection and facilitation for UNRWA personnel and operations, consistent with resolution 2720 (2023).
messages.Japan: Japan thanks Algeria for this constructive basis and supports the Council speaking clearly on the humanitarian catastrophe. To be balanced and effective, the text should explicitly condemn Hamas's 7 October terrorist attack and include an operative demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire leading to a sustainable cessation, alongside the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. We remain ready to engage constructively with all members.
messages.Malta: Malta supports the thrust of the Algerian draft and welcomes its focus on Rafah, hostages, humanitarian access, UNRWA and the ICJ. We ask that the immediate humanitarian ceasefire be placed in an operative paragraph, not only the preamble; that the text expressly condemn the Hamas terrorist attacks of 7 October and all terrorism; and that compliance with the ICJ's binding provisional measures be demanded, not merely called for. We would also like UNRWA's personnel and facilities to be explicitly protected in OP7.
messages.Mozambique: Mozambique supports the draft’s humanitarian focus and Algeria’s efforts. We ask that the immediate humanitarian ceasefire be placed in the operative part, not only the preamble, and that the Rafah paragraph be strengthened to prevent a military offensive that would deepen the catastrophe. These changes are consistent with our support for resolution 2720 and earlier ceasefire drafts and with the protection of civilians.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft’s humanitarian focus and is prepared to support it, but we ask that it explicitly condemn the 7 October terrorist attacks by Hamas and hostage-taking, and that OP4 call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire respected by all parties. We also propose reaffirming the right of all States to self-defence and the need to prevent terrorism, while stressing full compliance with international law. We hope these balanced additions can be reflected in the next revision.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports Algeria’s initiative, but the current text falls short of what the Council must demand: an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, not merely pauses or conditions for a later cessation. We also insist that the Council demand an end to Israeli military operations in Rafah and reject any forced displacement. We are ready to work constructively on this basis.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the draft's humanitarian and legal thrust, including the rejection of forced displacement and the call for compliance with the ICJ's provisional measures. Our priority is to ensure the Council does not only note the need for a ceasefire in the preamble: we ask the penholder to make OP4 demand an immediate humanitarian ceasefire respected by all parties. With that strengthening, Sierra Leone can support the text.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the draft as a basis, but the Council must operatively demand an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, not only humanitarian pauses, given the catastrophic situation. We also ask that OP5 be strengthened to explicitly prevent an Israeli military offensive in Rafah and that OP8 explicitly include UNRWA funding, as UNRWA remains indispensable to the humanitarian response. We can support the text with these changes.
messages.Switzerland: Switzerland supports the draft’s humanitarian focus and its balanced approach. We would like the immediate humanitarian ceasefire to be reflected in operative language, not only in the preamble, and a clear reference that the ICJ provisional measures are binding. These changes would strengthen the Council’s message on international law while preserving the text’s broader balance.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the draft's humanitarian objectives, including the demand for the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. To be able to support the text, we need an explicit condemnation of Hamas's terrorist attacks on 7 October, and we cannot accept language demanding an immediate humanitarian ceasefire. The text should instead refer to an immediate humanitarian pause and steps towards a sustainable cessation of hostilities.
messages.United States of America: The United States cannot support this text as drafted. We will veto any resolution that demands an immediate ceasefire without tying it to the release of hostages or that asks the Council to endorse the ICJ provisional measures. We need an explicit condemnation of Hamas's 7 October terrorist attacks and language making any ceasefire temporary and conditioned on hostages; with those changes we can engage constructively.

replies.France: partially accepted: ceasefire, Rafah and ICJ strengthened, but no explicit condemnation of Hamas.
replies.Japan: partially accepted: ceasefire included; explicit Hamas condemnation and hostage designation not included.
replies.Malta: partially accepted: ceasefire, ICJ and UNRWA included; explicit Hamas condemnation not included.
replies.Republic of Korea: partially accepted: ceasefire included; self-defence paragraph and explicit Hamas condemnation not included.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: rejected: retained immediate ceasefire and did not add explicit Hamas condemnation.
replies.United States of America: rejected: retained immediate ceasefire and ICJ references and declined hostage-conditioned ceasefire.

steps.summary: The revised text reflects Algeria's priorities: an operative immediate humanitarian ceasefire, cessation of Israeli operations in Rafah, binding ICJ compliance, protection and funding for UNRWA, and the two-State solution. It does not accept the US/UK red lines conditioning the ceasefire or deleting the ICJ reference, so the United States is expected to vote against and the United Kingdom to abstain.

messages.China: China supports the current text as it reflects the Council’s urgent responsibility to demand an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, ensure humanitarian access, protect civilians and medical facilities, and stop any Israeli military escalation in Rafah. The draft also reaffirms the two-State solution, support for UNRWA, and compliance with the ICJ’s provisional measures. We urge all Council members to support the text so that the Council can act without further delay.
messages.Ecuador: Ecuador thanks the penholder for incorporating our earlier requests, particularly the demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the call on Israel to cease military operations in Rafah, and compliance with the ICJ provisional measures. The text now reflects the urgency of the humanitarian catastrophe and the Council's responsibility. We support the draft as it stands and urge all members to unite behind it.
messages.France: France welcomes the strengthened language on an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, Rafah and the ICJ provisional measures, and remains prepared to support the text. However, the Council still cannot remain silent on the 7 October terrorist attacks by Hamas and other terrorist groups. France asks the penholder to add an explicit condemnation in the preamble; with that addition, France can vote in favour.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the revised draft as it stands. It reflects our red lines on an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, full compliance with the ICJ's binding provisional measures, and protection of UNRWA and humanitarian personnel, while addressing humanitarian access, hostages, Rafah and the two-State solution. We urge all Council members to vote in favour and call for full implementation without delay.
messages.Japan: Japan appreciates the inclusion of the immediate humanitarian ceasefire and sustained humanitarian access language, and we are ready to support the text. However, given the attacks of 7 October, Japan continues to believe the Council must explicitly condemn Hamas’s terrorism; we therefore ask to amend PP6 to name the 7 October terrorist attack while retaining the condemnation of all acts of terrorism. This is not a red line, but it would strengthen the resolution’s balance and clarity.
messages.Malta: Malta thanks Algeria for the revised text and supports it as presented. We continue to believe that an explicit condemnation of Hamas's terrorist attacks of 7 October 2023 would strengthen the Council's balance and unity, but we will not block a text that demands an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, humanitarian access and respect for the ICJ's provisional measures. Malta will vote in favour.
messages.Mozambique: Mozambique supports the revised draft as circulated. We welcome the incorporation of our previous requests on OP4 and OP5, which strengthen the call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and for an end to military operations in Rafah. The text reflects our priorities on civilian protection, humanitarian access, compliance with international law and the two-State solution. We urge Council unity and call on all members to support the draft.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea welcomes the inclusion of an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and remains ready to support a balanced, action-oriented text. For Council unity and to reflect the full context, we continue to seek an explicit condemnation of Hamas’s 7 October terrorist attacks and hostage-taking, as well as a reaffirmation of the right of self-defence exercised in conformity with international law. These additions would strengthen the text’s balance and humanitarian focus.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the revised draft. Our key red line on an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and our important request on Rafah have been reflected. We call on all Council members to vote in favour and send a clear signal on ending the suffering of civilians.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the revised draft and welcomes the incorporation of our OP4 amendment demanding an immediate humanitarian ceasefire. We urge the Council to unite behind this text and prioritize protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, compliance with international law, and the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the current text as revised and considers it responsive to the catastrophic situation on the ground. We welcome the inclusion of an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the clear demand regarding Rafah, and support for UNRWA’s ability to deliver assistance. We urge all Council members to support the draft and call for its urgent implementation, including the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages and full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access.
messages.Switzerland: Switzerland supports the current draft and thanks the penholder for accepting our earlier requests on OP4 and OP9. We welcome the clear demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and the recall that the ICJ's provisional measures are binding. Our support is based on the understanding that the humanitarian ceasefire is time-limited and does not prejudice Israel's right to ensure its defence and security. We urge all Council members to unite behind this text and all parties to comply with international humanitarian law and ensure unhindered humanitarian access.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: We appreciate the penholder's efforts and the urgency of the humanitarian situation. We cannot support the text as drafted. Our red lines remain: an explicit condemnation of Hamas's 7 October terrorist attacks and language on an immediate humanitarian pause rather than an immediate ceasefire. We also need OP8 to reflect the suspension of UK funding to UNRWA pending the independent review; an unqualified call to fund UNRWA is not acceptable.
messages.United States of America: The United States cannot support the draft as it stands. We reiterate our red lines: no demand for an immediate ceasefire, no ICJ provisional-measures language, and an explicit condemnation of Hamas's 7 October terrorist attacks. We also need OP4 recast as a hostage-linked temporary ceasefire and OP5 softened; otherwise we will not be able to vote in favor.

replies.France: rejected: current text already deplores all acts of terrorism; an explicit Hamas condemnation would unbalance the resolution and is not necessary to support a ceasefire.
replies.Japan: rejected: PP6 already deplores all attacks and terrorism; singling out one attack would undermine the resolution's balance.
replies.Republic of Korea: rejected: self-defence language could justify ongoing military operations; the existing text adequately addresses terrorism and hostages.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: rejected: replacing the immediate ceasefire with a pause and conditioning UNRWA funding would weaken core humanitarian demands.
replies.United States of America: rejected: removing the immediate ceasefire, ICJ references and softening Rafah would gut the resolution's purpose.

steps.summary: The revised text retains the immediate humanitarian ceasefire, Rafah cessation, ICJ compliance and UNRWA support as Algeria's core red lines. It rejects attempts to weaken these demands or add one-sided condemnations that would undermine balance. While 12 members are expected to vote in favour, the United States is expected to veto, preventing adoption.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria sponsored the draft and has consistently supported strong Council action on Palestine, so it votes in favour. It speaks before the vote to press for a ceasefire, humanitarian access, and Council responsibility despite expected US opposition.
reasons.China: China supports the Algerian draft’s immediate humanitarian ceasefire, protection of civilians, release of hostages, compliance with the ICJ, and unhindered humanitarian access, consistent with its prior positions. It would vote in favour and has not requested the floor before the vote.
reasons.Ecuador: Ecuador has consistently supported Council action on humanitarian access, ceasefire, and international law in this conflict, including similar drafts, and the resolution aligns with its stated priorities. It therefore votes yes despite known opposition from a permanent member.
reasons.France: France historically voted in favour of this Algeria-drafted ceasefire resolution while seeking a clearer condemnation of Hamas; it prioritised the humanitarian ceasefire and release of hostages despite the rejected amendment.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana supported the draft in the last negotiation round and has consistently backed immediate humanitarian ceasefire and international-law compliance. As the February Council President, Guyana would likely avoid a national statement before the vote.
reasons.Japan: Japan has repeatedly voted for Council action on a humanitarian ceasefire and hostage release, and despite the rejected amendment it sees this draft as a necessary humanitarian response consistent with its prior positions.
reasons.Malta: Malta has consistently voted in favour of ceasefire and humanitarian access texts, and it signalled support for this draft, which aligns with its stated policy on Gaza, hostages, civilian protection and the two-State solution.
reasons.Mozambique: Mozambique has consistently supported ceasefire and humanitarian draft resolutions on this agenda item, and this text aligns with its established positions on protection of civilians, humanitarian access, international law and the two-State solution.
reasons.Republic of Korea: ROK voted in favour of the Algeria-drafted ceasefire resolution on 20 February 2024; despite its rejected amendments, it supported urgent humanitarian action and aligned with the 13-1-1 outcome.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia consistently supported immediate humanitarian ceasefires and criticized US obstruction, so it would vote in favour and explain support before the vote.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone’s last negotiation position was support, and its foreign policy emphasizes humanitarian protection, international law, and a two-State solution, making a yes vote the most consistent choice.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia has consistently prioritized international humanitarian law, civilian protection, humanitarian access, and a ceasefire in Gaza, and the draft aligns with those positions, including the ICJ and two-State references. It would therefore vote in favour and explain its support before the vote.
reasons.Switzerland: Switzerland had already signalled support in negotiations and its foreign policy prioritizes international humanitarian law, civilian protection, hostage release, ICJ compliance, and two-State solution. The draft aligns with these priorities, so a yes vote with a pre-vote explanation is appropriate.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The draft omitted the UK’s red-line explicit condemnation of Hamas’s 7 October terrorist attacks and demanded an immediate ceasefire rather than the UK-backed humanitarian pause. The UK therefore abstained and is not expected to speak before the vote.
reasons.United States of America: The draft rejects every U.S. red line—unconditional ceasefire, ICJ references, no explicit Hamas condemnation, and intrusive Rafah language—so Washington would veto to protect ongoing hostage diplomacy and its alliance with Israel.

before.Algeria: Algeria will vote in favour of this draft resolution, which it has submitted because the Security Council cannot remain silent in the face of the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza. This text is balanced, firmly grounded in international law and the Charter, and reflects the urgent demands of the international community: an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, rejection of forced displacement, and compliance with the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. We especially warn against any military escalation in Rafah, where more than one million displaced civilians have sought refuge. The Council’s credibility is at stake. We call on all members to uphold their responsibilities and vote in favour, and we urge permanent members in particular not to block the Council from acting when the lives of civilians hang in the balance.
before.Ecuador: Ecuador will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza requires this Council to act with urgency and unity. We support the demands for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, respect for the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice, and progress towards a two-State solution. All parties must comply with international law, and this Council must not remain silent.
before.France: France will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian situation in Gaza is catastrophic and demands an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the unconditional release of all hostages, and full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale. France has consistently condemned the terrorist attacks of 7 October and stresses the need for accountability for all violations of international law. We regret that our request for an explicit condemnation of those attacks was not retained, but the Council cannot remain silent in the face of this emergency. France calls on all parties, including Israel, to comply strictly with international humanitarian law, to protect civilians everywhere, including in Rafah, and to implement the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. France reaffirms its commitment to the two-State solution.
before.Japan: Japan has consistently supported the Security Council’s efforts to respond to the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza and to secure the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. We regret that our proposed amendment explicitly condemning the heinous terrorist attack by Hamas on 7 October was not accepted, as clear condemnation of terrorism should be part of the Council’s response. Nonetheless, given the gravity of the crisis, especially the grave risk in Rafah, and the imperative to demand an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, Japan will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We call upon all parties to comply with international law and with the provisional measures of the International Court of Justice, and to uphold the vision of the two-State solution.
before.Mozambique: Mr. President, Mozambique will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, including the grave risks in Rafah, requires the Council to act with urgency and clarity. We support the demand for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, and the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel and facilities, including UNRWA. We also stress the obligation of all parties to comply with international law and with the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. Mozambique reiterates its commitment to the two-State solution, with Gaza as part of the Palestinian State and unified with the West Bank under the Palestinian Authority.
before.Republic of Korea: Mr. President, the Republic of Korea remains gravely concerned by the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza, especially the peril faced by more than one million civilians in Rafah. We have consistently called for the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and full respect for international humanitarian law. We would have preferred the text to expressly condemn the terrorist attacks by Hamas and other terrorist groups on 7 October and to reaffirm clearly the right of self-defence under international law. Nevertheless, given the urgency of alleviating the immense suffering and enabling humanitarian relief, the Republic of Korea will vote in favour of this draft resolution.
before.Russian Federation: Mr. President, the Russian Federation has consistently spoken in favour of an immediate cessation of hostilities in Gaza, the protection of civilians, and unimpeded humanitarian access. The draft before the Council responds to the overwhelming demand of the international community, including the Arab Group, for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the release of all hostages, the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and respect for the provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. We support the draft’s demand that Israel cease its military operations in Rafah, where more than one million civilians have sought refuge, and we reject any forced displacement of the Palestinian population. We regret that the Council has for months been prevented from taking the necessary action by the obstruction of certain members. The Russian Federation will vote in favour of this resolution.
before.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone votes in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, including the dire situation in Rafah, requires the Council to act with urgency and clarity. We support demands for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, respect for international humanitarian law and the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel. We also stress the binding nature of the provisional measures of the International Court of Justice and reaffirm our commitment to the two-State solution, with Gaza as part of a Palestinian State and a unified Palestinian Authority.
before.Slovenia: Slovenia will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, including the intolerable situation in Rafah, demands that this Council act with urgency and unity. We support the demands for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and full respect for international humanitarian law. We reject forced displacement and stress the binding nature of the International Court of Justice’s provisional measures. Slovenia also reaffirms its commitment to the two-State solution and to Gaza as part of a future Palestinian State. We call on all parties to comply immediately and on all Council members to support this text.
before.Switzerland: Switzerland will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza requires urgent action by this Council: the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure—including hospitals, schools, United Nations facilities and humanitarian personnel—and full compliance by all parties with international law, including the binding provisional measures indicated by the International Court of Justice. Switzerland is gravely concerned by the situation in Rafah and reiterates that forced displacement is prohibited. We have consistently supported urgent and extended humanitarian pauses and a sustainable cessation of hostilities, without prejudicing Israel’s legitimate security concerns, and we call on all parties to implement this resolution in full. Switzerland also stresses the essential humanitarian role of UNRWA and the need for adequate and predictable funding for the humanitarian response.
before.United States of America: The United States has engaged in good faith and shares the Council’s deep concern about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza. We continue to work intensively for the release of all hostages, expanded humanitarian access, and a temporary ceasefire linked to that release. But this draft is not balanced and will not advance those goals. It demands an immediate, unconditional ceasefire even as sensitive negotiations are under way to secure the hostages’ freedom. It fails to unequivocally condemn the terrorist attacks by Hamas and other terrorist groups against Israel on 7 October 2023. It also includes language on the International Court of Justice and on Rafah that we believe is unhelpful and could complicate ongoing diplomacy. The United States cannot support this text and will vote against it. We urge the Council to pursue a balanced resolution that condemns Hamas’s terrorism, demands the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, supports the negotiations, facilitates humanitarian assistance, and helps create the conditions for a sustainable cessation of hostilities.

after.Algeria:
Mr. President,

Algeria voted in favour of the draft resolution before the Council, and we deeply regret that, despite the overwhelming support of thirteen members, this balanced and credible text was not adopted because of the negative vote of a permanent member. We thank all delegations that supported the text and joined us in responding to the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza.

This is a sad day for the Security Council and a sad day for the Palestinian people. Once again, the Council has been prevented from shouldering its responsibilities. Once again, a veto has silenced the Council at a moment when civilians are being killed, hospitals are no longer functioning, more than a million displaced persons are sheltering in Rafah under the threat of further military escalation, and the humanitarian system is collapsing. The message sent today is a message of impunity, and it will be received with frustration, disappointment and despair by Palestinians and by all those who look to this Council as the custodian of international law.

The draft was not an extreme text. It demanded an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, the rejection of forced displacement, respect for international humanitarian law, and compliance with the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. It warned against a military operation in Rafah. It reaffirmed the two-State solution. These are not partisan demands; they are the minimum requirements of humanity and international law.

Algeria will continue to insist that the Security Council fulfil its Charter responsibilities. We call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, for an end to military operations in Rafah, for the opening of all crossings and the lifting of obstacles to humanitarian relief, for full support and protection of UNRWA and all humanitarian personnel, and for full compliance with the orders of the International Court of Justice. The veto cannot erase international law, and it cannot erase the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination and to a sovereign State, with Gaza as part of the Palestinian State and unified with the West Bank under the Palestinian Authority.

The Council must not remain silent. The killings must stop. The humanitarian catastrophe must end. Algeria will not tire in demanding that this Council act with courage, justice and consistency.
after.China: Mr. President, China voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Algeria. We thank Algeria and other Arab countries for their efforts to galvanise Council action in response to the catastrophic situation in Gaza. We express strong disappointment and regret that the draft resolution has again been vetoed by the United States. This text reflects the overwhelming call of the international community and the minimum demand of humanity: an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the unconditional release of all hostages, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, protection of civilians and civilian objects, respect for the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice, and rejection of forced displacement. The Council’s failure to act at this critical moment is deeply regrettable. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza continues to worsen. Over one million civilians are sheltering in Rafah, and any military escalation there would bring further untold suffering. China urges Israel, as the occupying Power, to immediately cease military operations in Gaza, especially to refrain from any ground operation in Rafah, to protect civilians and humanitarian and medical personnel and facilities, including UNRWA facilities, and to open all available crossings so that food, water, medicine, fuel and shelter can enter Gaza safely, rapidly and at scale. We demand the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages and safe humanitarian access to them. China calls for full implementation of resolution 2720 (2023), adequate funding for the humanitarian response including UNRWA, and compliance with the provisional measures ordered by the International Court of Justice. Forced displacement of the Palestinian civilian population must be rejected. The two-State solution, with Gaza as part of an independent Palestinian State and unified with the West Bank under the Palestinian Authority, remains the only way out. China will continue to stand on the side of justice and peace and to work for an immediate ceasefire and a just and lasting settlement of the Palestinian question.
after.Guyana:
Mr. President,

Guyana voted in favour of this draft resolution because the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza demands urgent, clear and principled action by this Council. We support the immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale, and the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, United Nations facilities, humanitarian personnel and UNRWA. We reject forced displacement and stress the obligation of all parties to comply with international law and with the binding provisional measures indicated by the International Court of Justice.

The situation in Rafah is especially alarming, with more than one million civilians seeking refuge. The Council cannot remain silent. Guyana regrets that this Council has again been unable to adopt a resolution calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire owing to the use of the veto. We urge all members to place the protection of civilian life, respect for the Charter and compliance with international humanitarian law above division, and to redouble efforts for an immediate ceasefire, humanitarian relief and a just and lasting two-State solution, with Gaza as part of a Palestinian State and unified with the West Bank under the Palestinian Authority.
after.Japan:
Mr. President,

Japan voted in favour of this draft resolution because the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza, including the grave and imminent risk in Rafah, requires urgent action by this Council. Japan regrets that the resolution was not adopted. The urgency on the ground cannot be allowed to fade simply because the Council could not act today.

Japan unequivocally condemns the heinous terrorist attacks by Hamas on 7 October and reiterates its demand for the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. At the same time, all parties must comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian objects, and ensure full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale. The provisional measures of the International Court of Justice must be fully respected.

Japan appreciates the intensive diplomatic efforts by the United States, Egypt, Qatar and other partners to achieve a ceasefire, secure the release of hostages and improve the humanitarian situation. We urge all Council members to overcome divisions and find common ground so that the Council can speak with one voice and make a tangible difference for civilians in Gaza. Japan remains fully committed to working with all partners towards a humanitarian ceasefire, the release of all hostages and the two-State solution.
after.Malta:
Mr President,
Malta voted in favour of this draft resolution and deeply regrets that it was not adopted. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza is intolerable, and this Council cannot remain silent. Malta has consistently condemned the brutal terrorist attacks by Hamas on 7 October and reiterates its demand for the immediate, safe and unconditional release of all hostages. All parties must comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian objects—including hospitals, schools, United Nations facilities, and humanitarian and medical personnel—and ensure full, rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access at scale throughout Gaza.

Malta supports the demands in the text for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire and for urgent steps to create the conditions for a sustainable cessation of hostilities. We are gravely concerned by the situation in Rafah, where more than one million civilians have sought refuge, and we oppose any military escalation that would further worsen the humanitarian catastrophe. We reject forced displacement in violation of international law. The provisional measures of the International Court of Justice are binding, and all parties must comply with them. Full implementation of resolutions 2712 (2023) and 2720 (2023) remains essential, including the full functioning of the Senior Humanitarian and Reconstruction Coordinator and a humanitarian mechanism that accelerates, rather than obstructs, the delivery of assistance. We reaffirm our support for UNRWA and for adequate and timely funding of the humanitarian response.

Malta remains firmly committed to the two-State solution, with Gaza as an integral part of the Palestinian State and unified with the West Bank under the Palestinian Authority. The Council’s responsibility is to help end the suffering, protect civilians and create a path towards a just and lasting peace. We urge all members to redouble efforts to that end.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr President,

The Russian Federation voted in favour of this draft resolution. It reflected the minimum that the Council could do, and the minimum demanded by the overwhelming majority of Member States, including the Arab Group: an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian access, release of all hostages, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, rejection of forced displacement, and compliance with the binding provisional measures of the International Court of Justice.

By vetoing this text, the United States has once again prevented the Security Council from discharging its responsibilities. This is not a dispute over a comma or a negotiating tactic. It is a cynical veto against the lives of Palestinian civilians, including more than one million people seeking refuge in Rafah. Washington has blocked the Council’s demand to stop the fighting and to halt preparations for a ground operation in Rafah that would produce a new humanitarian catastrophe.

We have heard once again about ongoing diplomatic efforts and about the need not to complicate them. But this argument has been used for months. And for months the Council has remained paralysed while the humanitarian situation in Gaza has become catastrophic. The United States is effectively shielding the Israeli military operation from any Council action. It has become complicit in the collective punishment of the Palestinian population. The blood of those who could have been saved is increasingly on the hands of those who repeatedly block the Council’s calls for a ceasefire.

The Russian Federation has consistently condemned all acts of terrorism and all attacks against civilians, including those on 7 October. But no act of terrorism can justify the indiscriminate destruction of Gaza, the killing of tens of thousands of civilians, the destruction of hospitals and UN facilities, or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people. International humanitarian law applies to all parties without exception. The decisions of the International Court of Justice are binding and must be implemented, not ignored.

Today’s veto does not give Israel impunity, and it does not absolve the United States of responsibility. The Council cannot remain hostage to the position of one permanent member. We will continue to demand an immediate ceasefire, full humanitarian access, the release of all hostages, and a just settlement of the Palestinian question on the basis of the two-State solution, with East Jerusalem as the capital of a sovereign Palestinian State and Gaza as an integral part of it.

The veto has blocked the Council, but it cannot block the truth. The international community sees clearly who is obstructing the cessation of hostilities. The Russian Federation will continue to work with all responsible members of the Council and with the wider membership to ensure that the Council upholds the Charter and does not remain silent in the face of this catastrophe.

Thank you.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
Thank you, Mr President. The United Kingdom abstained on this draft resolution. We did so with regret, because we share the Council’s deep concern at the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza. The United Kingdom has been clear: we need an immediate humanitarian pause to get aid in and hostages out, leading to a sustainable ceasefire. We have called on Israel to comply with international humanitarian law, to protect civilians—including those sheltering in Rafah—and to allow much more aid through more crossings. We have tripled our aid and are working with partners to deliver it.

But the resolution before us was not balanced. It did not explicitly condemn the Hamas terrorist attacks of 7 October, and it did not make clear that a ceasefire must be sustainable and cannot leave Hamas able to carry out such attacks again. An immediate, unconditional ceasefire, rather than a pause linked to the release of hostages and a diplomatic process, would not advance the goal of ending this conflict. The United Kingdom continues to call for the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages and for safe, unhindered humanitarian access at scale. We support the ongoing mediation by Egypt, Qatar and the United States and urge all parties to seize it. We will remain actively engaged in the Council and with partners to reach a sustainable ceasefire, protect civilians, and advance the two-State solution.
after.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States fully shares the Council’s grave concern at the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza. We have worked intensively to secure the release of all hostages, to expand humanitarian access, and to create the conditions for a temporary ceasefire that would allow aid to reach Palestinian civilians at scale. That is why we could not support this draft resolution. It demands an immediate and unconditional ceasefire while sensitive negotiations are under way to secure the hostages’ release—negotiations that remain the most realistic path to a pause in the fighting and to a major scaling-up of humanitarian assistance. The text also failed to unequivocally condemn the terrorist attacks by Hamas and other terrorist groups on 7 October, and it did not link a ceasefire to the release of hostages. The Council must be clear: there can be no ceasefire that leaves hostages in captivity. The United States will continue its diplomacy with Egypt, Qatar, Israel, and other partners. We remain ready to work with Council members on a resolution that advances the release of hostages, expands humanitarian access, protects civilians and humanitarian personnel, and supports a durable path toward the two-State solution. We continue to insist that all parties comply with international humanitarian law, and we have made clear our concerns about any military operation in Rafah without a credible and implementable plan to protect the civilians there. The United States remains committed to the two-State solution and to a future in which Israelis and Palestinians live in peace and security. We regret that the Council could not unite behind a text that reflected those priorities, but we will not support a resolution that, in our judgment, would jeopardize the best remaining opportunity to bring the hostages home and secure a real pause that can ease the suffering of Palestinian civilians.
